system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.

patient presented with elevated BNP and CXR with moderate 
pulmonary edema concerning for diastolic heart failure

medication non-adherence or dietary indiscretion. The patient

worsening MR and TR as well as possibly worsened RV systolic

been overestimated).   After the lasix drip, she was treated

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I know you're feeling very short of breath. We're going to help you. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t breathe… it’s been getting worse for two days. My nebulizer broke, so I couldn’t use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your oxygen levels are very low, and your CO2 is extremely high. We’re going to help you breathe, but you may need a breathing tube temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No… I don’t want that. I just need air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but your body isn’t removing CO2 properly. Without help, you could pass out. We’re trying BiPAP first, but if it doesn’t work, we may need to intubate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t… it’s suffocating me…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is worsening. You’re becoming too sleepy to keep your airway safe. We’re going to sedate you and place a breathing tube now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No… please…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The team has placed the breathing tube. You're in the ICU now. You’re on a ventilator to help you breathe. Your heart slowed down during the procedure, but we gave medication to support it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re still on the ventilator. Your chest X-ray shows fluid in your lungs from heart failure and COPD. We’re giving diuretics to help remove the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I breathe on my own yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Your CO2 was 110 when you arrived—very high. We’re slowly improving that. Your heart function is okay, but your lungs need more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is improving. The X-ray shows less fluid. We’re reducing the ventilator support. We’ll try to remove the tube soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Can I get off the machine today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll assess you today. But we need to be sure you can clear CO2 on your own. Your heart rhythm was unstable earlier—we think you may have sick sinus syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart’s natural pacemaker isn’t working well. You had a slow rhythm after intubation. We used dopamine to support your blood pressure. It’s stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—we removed the breathing tube this morning. You’re breathing on your own with oxygen. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better… but tired. My chest feels clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your lungs are improving. We’re continuing diuretics to reduce fluid. Your kidney function dipped due to the diuretics, but it’s recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the floor today. You’ll need to use your nebulizer regularly. We’ve arranged for a new machine—yours will be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t realize how much I needed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We need to talk. Last night, you stopped breathing and became unresponsive. It happened after you refused to wear your CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t like the mask… it felt like drowning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But with your COPD and obesity, your body can’t maintain oxygen and CO2 levels without it. You were brought back to the ICU for monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need it… but maybe there’s a better fit?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll get you evaluated for a more comfortable mask. It could prevent future hospitalizations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started antibiotics. Your urine culture grew Enterococcus—resistant to vancomycin. We believe you have a kidney infection, which caused confusion earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was confused? I don’t remember.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had altered mental status and fever. The antibiotics are working—your labs are improving. You’ll finish a course at home with linezolid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped fluoxetine and trazodone because they can interact with linezolid. Your depression meds are adjusted—lamotrigine is restarted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is stable. We’re weaning oxygen. Your weight is down from 131.6 kg to 126 kg—good progress on fluid removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter. But my legs are a bit swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have mild pitting edema—common with heart and kidney issues. We’ll keep monitoring. Your torsemide dose is now twice daily to maintain balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your echocardiogram shows your heart’s squeezing function is preserved, but you have increased pressure on the left side—consistent with your heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my heart is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s stiff—diastolic dysfunction. That’s why fluid backs up into your lungs. Staying on diuretics and managing salt is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff test came back negative—good news. We’ll continue your antibiotics and insulin. Your blood sugar has been high, so we increased your Lantus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying to eat less sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That helps. We’ll keep adjusting insulin. Your kidney function is improving—creatinine down to 1.1 from a peak of 1.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Palliative care spoke with you yesterday. You confirmed you want full treatment, even if you’re unable to decide during a crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I want everything done. My brother is my contact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’ll make sure your wishes are documented. You’re doing well—likely to go home in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows improving lung opacities—likely resolving infection or atelectasis. No pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your infection is clearing, breathing is better, and heart failure is controlled. We’re focusing on discharge planning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re down to 3L oxygen and feeling strong. We’ll try stopping oxygen today and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I can manage without it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s monitor. Also, please weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds—it could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your oxygen is off, and you walked to the hallway. Discharge is likely tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue linezolid for 14 days, use your new nebulizer, wear CPAP at night, take torsemide twice daily, and monitor weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—metoprolol, aspirin, simvastatin, and rivaroxaban are all restarted. Candesartan will be added once your kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more day. Your labs are stable. We’re arranging home services for nursing and CPAP setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I didn’t know how serious it was.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a close call, but you’re on the mend. Staying on top of your treatments will help prevent another crisis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary. Call if you have trouble breathing, weight gain, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you—for not giving up on me, even when I didn’t want help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of COPD, diastolic heart failure, and morbid obesity was admitted for severe dyspnea after her nebulizer broke and she stopped treatments. She developed hypercapnic respiratory failure with a pCO2 of 110 and pH of 7.09, requiring intubation. She was treated for acute on chronic diastolic heart failure with diuresis, which led to acute kidney injury that resolved. During hospitalization, she had bradycardia with junctional rhythm, consistent with sick sinus syndrome, supported with dopamine. After extubation, she had an episode of apnea due to CPAP noncompliance, requiring ICU monitoring. A urine culture grew vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus, and she was treated for presumed pyelonephritis with linezolid. Her condition stabilized over 15 days, and she was discharged home on oral antibiotics, diuretics, and with plans for CPAP re-evaluation and heart failure follow-up.
